statement: An environment has weakly homogeneous agents if, for any joint policy and any permutation sigma of agent identities, agent i's expected utility under the original assignment equals agent sigma(i)'s utility under the permuted joint policy (Definition 14, Eq. 9.86) -- i.e., agent identities/policies can be relabeled across agents without changing induced returns.
conditions: defined for any joint policy pi and any permutation sigma over the fixed agent index set I
limits: does not by itself imply agents should act identically under the optimal policy

statement: An environment has strongly homogeneous agents (Definition 15) if it has weakly homogeneous agents and the optimal joint policy pi* consists of identical individual policies pi1 = pi2 = ... = pin.
conditions: requires weak homogeneity plus identical-policy optimality of the joint policy
limits: the authors note this is a strong assumption that can be difficult to verify in a given environment

statement: Parameter sharing sets theta_shared = theta1 = ... = thetan and/or phi_shared = phi1 = ... = phin (Eq. 9.87) across all agents' networks, which constrains the joint policy to consist of identical individual policies and directly aligns with the strongly-homogeneous-agents assumption (Definition 15).
conditions: applies to policy and/or value-function network parameters
limits: none stated in the equation itself; caveats given separately

statement: Parameter sharing keeps the number of learned parameters constant regardless of the number of agents n, whereas not sharing parameters causes a linear increase in the number of parameters with n; sharing also lets shared parameters train on the pooled, more diverse experience of all agents.
conditions: stated as a general benefit of parameter sharing, not tied to a specific experiment
limits: benefit is conditioned on the environment plausibly having strongly homogeneous agents

statement: The text does not claim parameter sharing is beneficial in environments that are only weakly (not strongly) homogeneous. In the weakly-homogeneous two-landmark example (Figure 9.23a), the optimal joint policy requires agents to behave differently, so imposing the parameter-sharing constraint (Eq. 9.87) prevents learning that optimal joint policy.
conditions: specific to environments with weakly but not strongly homogeneous agents
limits: a single illustrative environment, not a general impossibility proof

statement: Augmenting each agent's observation with its own index i (giving observation obar^t_i) theoretically allows shared parameters to still express distinct per-agent behavior, but the authors state that in practice this may not be sufficient because a shared network's representational capacity might not be enough to encode several distinct strategies from an index alone, citing Christianos et al. (2021) on the limitations of parameter sharing with and without an index observation.
conditions: index-augmented observation under continued full parameter sharing
limits: the authors explicitly flag this as a practical limitation, not a solved problem

statement: In a level-based foraging environment (6x6 grid, two level-1 agents, one level-2 item), four independent-A2C parameter-sharing configurations (full, critic-only, actor-only, none) were compared; sharing parameters led to convergence in fewer environment time steps, but did not necessarily increase final converged returns since all four variants reached similar policies in this example (Figure 9.24).
evidence_type: empirical figure reproduced from cited paper
conditions: single small level-based foraging instance (6x6 grid, 2 agents, 1 item), independent A2C base algorithm
limits: single environment configuration; final returns converged similarly across all four variants in this instance, so speed-of-convergence and final-performance effects of sharing are not the same claim

statement: Experience sharing trains a separate parameter set per agent but pools trajectories across agents (e.g., a single shared replay buffer D_shared for DQN, Algorithm 24); this relaxes the strongly-homogeneous-agents assumption to weak homogeneity, since agents are not constrained to identical policies. Merely replacing individual buffers with a shared one, without also increasing the number of samples drawn per training step, does not by itself change learning versus individual buffers.
conditions: off-policy algorithms (DQN family) can directly use transitions collected by other agents
limits: the stated benefit requires also increasing the number of backpropagation/sampling steps performed per environment step, not just pooling the buffer

statement: Shared experience actor-critic (SEAC) (Christianos, Schafer, and Albrecht 2020) applies experience sharing to on-policy algorithms (e.g., A2C, PPO) by treating other agents' trajectories as off-policy data and correcting for this with importance sampling (Eq. 9.88-9.89); the sharing weight hyperparameter lambda controls the contribution of others' experience, with lambda=1 weighting it equally to one's own and lambda=0 collapsing to no sharing.
conditions: on-policy actor-critic algorithms; requires importance-sampling correction because other agents' data is generated by different (off-policy) policies
limits: equation_text_unreliable: the big-operator glyphs in Eq. 9.88-9.89 extracted unreliably and were not re-typeset

statement: Experience sharing is stated to be more computationally expensive per environment step than parameter sharing (larger batches, per-agent parameter counts that scale with the number of agents n), and unlike parameter sharing it does not assume the optimal joint policy is composed of identical individual policies.
conditions: comparison is between experience sharing and parameter sharing specifically, not against no-sharing baselines
limits: a qualitative cost/assumption trade-off statement, not a quantitative benchmark

statement: Policy self-play, as presented in Section 9.8, is scoped to two-agent, fully observable, zero-sum, turn-taking games and requires that the agents in the game have symmetrical roles and egocentric observations so that a single trained policy can be used to select actions from the perspective of each agent.
section: 9.8 Policy Self-Play in Zero-Sum Games / 9.8.2 Self-Play MCTS
conditions: two agents, zero-sum, turn-taking, fully observable states/actions, symmetric roles, egocentric observation representation available
limits: explicitly stated by the authors as a requirement of the method, not merely a convenient special case; general-sum or non-symmetric-role extension is deferred to Section 9.9

statement: For chess self-play, the state s = (i, x, y) (agent-to-move index, that agent's piece locations, the opponent's piece locations) is transformed via psi(s) = (1, y, x) to reuse agent 1's policy pi1 to act for agent 2; this transformation corresponds geometrically to rotating the board 180 degrees and swapping piece colors (Figure 9.26).
conditions: specific to the chess state representation given (agent index plus own/opponent piece-location vectors)
limits: worked example for one game; the general mechanism requires only that egocentric observations and a shared action set can be defined

statement: The general Monte Carlo tree search algorithm for MDPs (Algorithm 25) selects actions during simulation via UCB (Eq. 9.90), which assumes rewards lie in the normalized range [0,1], and its finite-sample estimation errors are bounded when used in MCTS, citing Kocsis and Szepesvari (2006).
conditions: UCB action selection requires rewards normalized to [0,1]; the finite-sample bound is attributed to a separate cited work, not proved in this text
limits: the book states the bound exists and cites the source, but does not reproduce the proof

statement: AlphaZero learns a joint policy-value network f(s;theta) = (u, p) (Eq. 9.93) from self-play alone, starting from randomly initialized parameters, minimizing the combined loss L(theta) = (z-u)^2 - pi^T log p + c||theta||^2 (Eq. 9.94) via SGD over self-play data D = {(s_t, pi_t, z_T)}, where pi_t is the MCTS visit-count action distribution and z_T is the eventual game outcome.
section: 9.8.3 Self-Play MCTS with Deep Neural Networks: AlphaZero
conditions: two-player zero-sum turn-taking games with fully observable state; MCTS search guided by the learned p; requires random initialization and iterative self-play data generation
limits: equation_text_unreliable noted for this chunk (big-operator/summation glyphs in surrounding equations); full implementation detail (network architecture, exploration schedule, action masking) is explicitly deferred to the original paper

statement: Reported AlphaZero match results (Figure 9.27, from Silver et al. 2018) when playing white: vs. Stockfish (chess) 29.0% win / 70.6% draw / 0.4% loss; vs. Elmo (shogi) 84.2% win / 2.2% draw / 13.6% loss; vs. AlphaGo Zero trained for three days (Go) 68.9% win / 31.1% loss (no draw reported). Each AlphaZero instance used k=800 MCTS simulations per state and trained for 9 hours/44M games (chess), 12 hours/24M games (shogi), 13 days/140M games (Go).
evidence_type: empirical figure reproduced from cited paper
conditions: results as reported by Silver et al. (2018); AlphaZero playing white against the stated opponent programs
limits: these are the authors' reproduction of externally reported match statistics, not a result generated by Albrecht et al. themselves

statement: Policy space response oracles (PSRO) construct, in each generation k, a meta-game M^k -- a finite normal-form game whose per-agent action set is that agent's current policy population Pi^k_i and whose payoffs are empirically estimated expected returns of the underlying game G -- then use a meta-solver (e.g., Nash equilibrium) to obtain population distributions delta^k_i, and an oracle (typically an approximate best response trained via single-agent RL, Eq. 9.96) to add a new policy to each population (Eq. 9.97).
conditions: general-sum games with full or partial observability, two or more agents (any POSG or other Chapter 3 game model)
limits: equation_text_unreliable noted for this chunk

statement: If PSRO uses a meta-solver that computes exact Nash equilibria and an oracle that computes exact best-response policies, then in a finite underlying game the population distributions {delta^k_i} converge, and if PSRO converges the outcome is guaranteed to be a Nash equilibrium of the underlying game; the argument relies on finite games always admitting deterministic best responses and having a finite enumerable set of deterministic policies.
conditions: finite underlying game G (finite agents, actions, states, observations, terminating in finite time); exact meta-game payoffs (Ri = Ui); exact best-response oracle
limits: the authors explicitly state both idealized assumptions (exact meta-games, exact best responses) will likely not hold in practice, since meta-games are estimated from finitely many sampled episodes and best responses are learned via RL

statement: The stated PSRO convergence-to-Nash-equilibrium result is not evidence that a practical, sampled-meta-game / RL-trained-best-response implementation of PSRO converges to Nash equilibrium; the authors themselves note the exactness assumptions underlying the proof sketch will likely not hold in practice.
conditions: applies to any real PSRO run using sampled episodes and RL-trained best responses
limits: the authors do cite a bound (Tuyls et al. 2020) on sample counts needed for approximate transfer of Nash equilibria from estimated to exact meta-games, so the gap is not left entirely unaddressed in the literature

statement: AlphaStar uses League training: a single per-race league Pi^k containing three agent types (main agents, main exploiter agents, league exploiter agents) distinguished by their opponent-sampling distribution via prioritized fictitious self-play (PFSP, Eq. 9.98), by when their policy snapshots are frozen into the league, and by when/whether their parameters are reset to the supervised-pretraining initialization.
section: 9.9.3 Grandmaster Level in StarCraft II: AlphaStar
conditions: per-race training (Terran, Protoss, Zerg); requires prior supervised pretraining on human replay data to seed the policies before League RL training
limits: equation_text_unreliable noted for this chunk

statement: AlphaStar's final trained main agents reached Grandmaster level in the full game of StarCraft II, ranked above 99.8 percent of officially ranked human players; supervised-only (pre-RL) initial policies already ranked above 84 percent of human players; the authors report that without human-replay pretraining, AlphaStar's performance degrades substantially because the roughly 10^26-action search space becomes too difficult to explore from scratch (Vinyals et al. 2019).
section: 9.9.3 Grandmaster Level in StarCraft II: AlphaStar
evidence_type: empirical figure reproduced from cited paper
conditions: evaluation via the official StarCraft II online match-making system under an anonymous account; main agents evaluated without conditioning on the strategy statistic z; pretraining used a 971,000-match anonymized human replay dataset of top-22-percent MMR players
limits: reported results are the authors' summary of Vinyals et al. (2019), not independently reproduced by Albrecht et al.

statement: Deep joint-action learning (Algorithm 23) has each agent i train neural-network agent models pi-hat^i_j of every other agent j by minimizing a cross-entropy loss against j's true observed action (Eq. 9.80), plus a centralized action-value function Q(h_i, <a_i,a_-i>; theta_i) whose target uses the greedy action of agent i weighted by the product of other agents' predicted action probabilities, either computed exactly (Eq. 9.82-9.83) or approximated by sampling K joint actions from the agent models (Eq. 9.84) to avoid summing over all joint actions of other agents.
section: 9.6.1 Joint-Action Learning with Deep Agent Models
conditions: partially observable environments (POSGs); agents need access to other agents' actions during training but only their own observation history at execution time
limits: equation_text_unreliable noted for this chunk; exact target computation is intractable for many agents or large action spaces, motivating the sampling approximation

statement: In a two-agent level-based foraging environment requiring cooperation to collect items, IDQN fails to reliably learn policies that collect items, whereas JAL-AM (both exact and K=10-sampled target computation) learns to collect items; the sampled variant learns faster and more reliably than the exact variant, which the authors attribute to the sampled variant prioritizing value estimates for the other agent's more commonly taken (better-trained) actions and to additional exploratory noise from sampling.
section: 9.6.1 Joint-Action Learning with Deep Agent Models
evidence_type: empirical figure reproduced from cited paper
conditions: level-based foraging, two agents, 2M environment steps, learning rate 3e-4, batch size 128, gamma=0.99, epsilon-greedy annealed 1 to 0.05, target networks updated every 200 steps, replay buffer of 100,000 transitions, results averaged over 5 seeds
limits: single small environment configuration; the explanation for why the sampled variant outperforms the exact variant is offered as a plausible mechanism ("likely due to"), not proven

statement: The entire chapter (Section 9.10 summary and the material in this reader's range) formulates every algorithm -- independent learning, centralized critics, value decomposition, agent modeling, parameter/experience sharing, self-play, and population-based training -- over a fixed, known agent set/index i in {1,...,n}; none of the material in pdf pages 295-333 establishes generalization of any of these algorithms to a variable or held-out number of agents N.
conditions: applies to all algorithms covered in Chapter 9 pages 295-333: JAL-AM, agent-model representation learning, parameter sharing, experience sharing/SEAC, AlphaZero, PSRO, AlphaStar
limits: an absence claim about this specific page range only; earlier or later chapters (outside this reader's assignment) are not checked

statement: Parameter sharing's stated property of keeping parameter count constant as agent count n grows (Eq. 9.87 and surrounding discussion, p. 305-306) is the textbook analogue of the scaling behavior an N-agnostic shared-policy design (such as HMASD's skill-conditioned policy) seeks, but the authors' own caveat that strong homogeneity is a strong, hard-to-verify assumption is a boundary condition on how far that analogy extends to heterogeneous or variable-role rosters.
conditions: prospective; not validated against any HMASD result
limits: this is a curator-labeled connection, not a source claim; it must not be read as evidence that HMASD's design satisfies strong homogeneity

statement: Self-play's explicit requirement of symmetric roles and egocentric observations for a single shared policy to act for every agent (Section 9.8.2, p. 315) is a candidate boundary condition to check against any HMASD design that reuses one policy across agents with potentially different roles or skill assignments.
conditions: prospective; not validated against any HMASD result
limits: this is a curator-labeled connection, not a source claim; the book's self-play requirement is stated only for two-agent zero-sum games, not for general multi-agent skill-conditioned policies
